title: T. Rex Body Temperature Was Similar to Our Own
paragraphs: T. rex may have disappeared some 66 million years ago, but scientists have finally taken its temperature — and found that the giant predator ran almost as warm as we do.
Of course, they could not exactly put a thermometer under a dinosaur's tongue, but fossilized teeth gave them the next best thing!

Scientists once believed dinosaurs were sluggish, cold-blooded creatures. Later discoveries changed that view, and most researchers now agree that dinosaurs such as T. rex were warm-blooded and could control their body temperature.
Scientists previously looked for answers by studying dinosaur bones and how T. rex grew. In a new study, researchers turned to chemical clues preserved in its teeth.

Atoms in tooth enamel group together in different patterns depending on an animal's body temperature. By examining these patterns in three T. rex teeth, the researchers calculated that the dinosaur had an average body temperature of about 36 degrees Celsius.
That is similar to the temperature of modern elephants and close to the normal human range of 36 to 37 degrees Celsius.
The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

"I almost would have expected a higher body temperature," said Jasmina Wiemann, a paleobiologist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the study. Based on her own research, she thought T. rex might have been a few degrees warmer, like modern birds — the descendants of dinosaurs.

Knowing T. rex's body temperature could help scientists better understand how it lived. Researchers say its ability to maintain a stable internal temperature may have allowed it to survive across most of prehistoric North America, including both cooler and hotter regions.
The discovery could also offer clues about how active T. rex was, how much food it needed and the animals it hunted to meet its energy needs.
Researchers now hope to use the same method to take the temperatures of other dinosaur species.
